title: Coastal Migratory Pelagic Resources of the Gulf and Atlantic Region; Re-Opening of Commercial Harvest for Atlantic Spanish Mackerel in the Northern Zone
summary:
The federal government just issued two updates: tighter rules for how states handle commercial truck licenses for people who live outside the United States, and short-term adjustments to East Coast fishing seasons and quotas for Spanish mackerel and bluefish.

On trucking, states now must verify documents more rigorously before issuing or changing commercial learner permits and licenses for applicants who are domiciled in another country. States must keep copies of all related paperwork, including proof of lawful immigration status, for at least two years and be able to share them with the federal trucking regulator within 48 hours if asked. States have to be in substantial compliance with these rules starting September 29, 2025, before they issue, renew, transfer, or upgrade any such permits or licenses.

Who benefits: employers and the public get stronger safeguards against fraud, and consistent standards across states. Legitimate drivers should see clearer, more uniform expectations. Who may feel the impact: state motor vehicle agencies face added workload and recordkeeping; applicants who live outside the country may experience more steps and possible delays, and some will have concerns about how their personal documents are stored and shared.

On fisheries, the federal fisheries agency is reopening commercial harvest of Spanish mackerel in the northern zone from September 29 through October 6 because extra quota was shifted from the southern zone. After those eight days, the northern zone will close again through the end of the current fishing year. In a separate move, New Jersey transferred part of its 2025 bluefish quota to North Carolina to help balance catch with demand.

Who benefits: commercial fishers, dealers, and coastal businesses in the northern states get a short window to land more Spanish mackerel, and North Carolina’s bluefish fleet gains room to operate legally without overshooting limits. Who may be negatively affected: southern mackerel fishers see less quota this year, New Jersey’s bluefish fleet has a smaller share, and buyers could see brief swings in supply. The quick reopening and re-closing may also complicate planning for small operators.

Overall, these steps aim to tighten identity and eligibility checks in trucking and fine-tune fish harvests so the seasons match real-world conditions while staying within conservation limits. The trade-offs are more administrative work and tighter timelines for some, and a bit of short-term uncertainty for parts of the fishing industry.
